question: Family farms dominate EU agriculture in terms of farm numbers, their contribution to agricultural employment and, to a lesser extent, the surface area being farmed and the production value they generate. Almost six out of ten farms (around 57%) are run by the owner and family members alone. In another 36% of farms, family members made up at least 50% of the total workforce.

Family farms accounted for the largest share of the agricultural surface area in 2020 (around 61% of the 157.4 million hectares used), the majority of the total agricultural labour force (almost 78%), more than half of all livestock farms (almost 55%) and more than half of the standard agricultural output (around 56%).

However, without the necessary support, these farms are liable to disappear, since new generations are not interested in careers in agriculture. Between 2005 and 2020 over 37% of farms have disappeared, and that decline unless we come up with viable solutions. 1.
What specific measures and initiatives is the Commission considering to support family farms in the future?
How effective are the current strategies for attracting young people into agriculture?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.2.2024) 1. Family farms are the backbone of European agriculture, and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) helps in keeping family farms throughout the EU territory. Without the CAP the decrease in the number of farms would be higher and we would lose our traditional rural landscapes.

The last evaluation of CAP considers that direct income support helps in stabilising farm income, with both pillars of the CAP playing an important role through various tools that address different needs and challenges. The Scenar 2020 study1 demonstrates that without CAP the most obvious effect would be a faster decline in the number of farms, and to a lesser degree in the area of land under agriculture.

Therefore, food production would be concentrated in large, industrial farms, with consequences for rural employment and rural livelihoods. 2. Generational renewal in agriculture is one of the ten objectives of the CAP. Member States must dedicate a minimum amount to support young farmers corresponding to 3% of their direct payments’ envelope.
Flexibility is granted as to which tools they can use for this financial package: enhanced income support, start-up aid for new young farmers or investment support with higher co-financing rates.

The last evaluation of CAP on generational renewal finds that the impact of CAP generational-renewal measures on the number of young farmers is positive but access to land and capital are the main barriers to entering the farming sector for young people. Facilitating access to land and capital may also require changes to improve the coherence of national policies with CAP generational renewal goals.
In addition, the new CAP, at the initiative of European Parliament, has extended support for installation of new farmers in addition to young farmers.
